items.title: Higher derivatives and the classes $C^k$ and $C^\infty$
items.strategy: Define $f^{(0)}=f$ and recursively $f^{(j+1)}=(f^{(j)})'$ wherever the latter derivative exists. Define $k$-times differentiability, $C^k$ on an interval (derivatives through order $k$ exist and are continuous, with the published one-sided endpoint convention), and $C^\infty$. State explicitly that $\mathbb N$ contains $0$, so $C^0$ means continuity, and prove the nesting $C^{k+1}\subseteq C^k$. Do not silently identify existence of $f^{(k)}$ with continuity of that derivative.

items.title: The general Leibniz rule for the $n$-th derivative of a product
items.strategy: For $n\in\mathbb N$ and sufficiently differentiable $f,g$, prove $(fg)^{(n)}=\sum_{j\le n}\iota\!\binom{n}{j}f^{(j)}g^{(n-j)}$. Induct on $n$, differentiate the finite sum termwise, shift one index, and combine adjacent coefficients with Pascal's rule. Keep binomial coefficients and factorials in $\mathbb N$ and insert the canonical embedding $\iota$ before multiplying real values.

items.title: Higher-order Rolle theorem
items.strategy: Given an explicitly ordered list $x_0<\cdots<x_n$ of zeros in an interval and an $n$-times differentiable function on the intervening interval, prove that its $n$-th derivative vanishes somewhere between the extreme zeros. Apply Rolle between consecutive listed zeros and iterate; state the exact endpoint continuity and interior differentiability assumptions inherited at each stage. Use induction, with $n=0$ treated separately.

items.title: Darboux's theorem: every derivative has the intermediate-value property
items.strategy: Let $f$ be differentiable on an interval and let $x<y$. For a value $\lambda$ strictly between $f'(x)$ and $f'(y)$, apply the extreme-value theorem to $h(t)=f(t)-\lambda t$. Difference quotients at the endpoints force a minimum or maximum away from both endpoints, and Fermat gives $h'(c)=0$. Handle equality at an endpoint separately and preserve the published one-sided derivative convention.

items.title: A derivative has neither a removable discontinuity nor a jump discontinuity
items.strategy: Combine Darboux's theorem with the published classification of discontinuities. A finite punctured limit different from the value and unequal finite one-sided limits each leave an omitted interval of values near the point, contradicting the intermediate-value property. Do not claim that every discontinuity of a derivative is a jump; discontinuities of the second kind remain possible.

items.title: An injective Darboux function on an interval is strictly monotone
items.strategy: For an injective function with the intermediate-value property, show that any three points $x<y<z$ force $f(y)$ to lie strictly between $f(x)$ and $f(z)$; otherwise the intermediate-value property on one of the two subintervals repeats a value. Deduce a globally consistent order orientation and hence strict monotonicity. Include the nondegenerate-interval and singleton cases.

items.title: An injective or monotone derivative on an interval is continuous
items.strategy: Darboux makes the derivative's image on every subinterval an interval. In the injective case first use the injective-Darboux lemma to obtain strict monotonicity; in either case apply the published theorem that a monotone function with interval image is continuous. This is the valid partial converse. Do not include the false claim that Darboux plus Baire class one implies continuity.

items.title: Cauchy's mean-value theorem in quotient form when the denominator derivative is nonzero
items.strategy: From the published cross-multiplied Cauchy mean-value theorem obtain $(f(x)-f(a))/(g(x)-g(a))=f'(c)/g'(c)$. Prove both denominators are nonzero: $g'(c)\ne0$ is assumed, while $g(x)=g(a)$ would contradict Rolle. State the one-sided endpoint version used by L'Hôpital and do not divide before these facts are established.

items.title: L'Hôpital's rule for the $0/0$ form at finite or infinite, one-sided endpoints
items.strategy: State a single theorem covering a finite one-sided endpoint and $\pm\infty$: $f,g$ tend to $0$, are differentiable in the punctured approach region, $g'$ never vanishes there, and $f'/g'$ tends to $L\in\overline{\mathbb R}$; then $f/g\to L$. At a finite endpoint extend both functions by $0$ and apply the quotient Cauchy theorem. Reduce $+\infty$ and $-\infty$ to the corresponding one-sided limit at $0$ by $t=1/x$; the chain-rule factors $-1/t^2$ cancel in the derivative quotient. Give separate order estimates for finite and infinite $L$.

items.title: L'Hôpital's rule for the $\infty/\infty$ form at finite or infinite, one-sided endpoints
items.strategy: Assume $|g|\to\infty$, the numerator has a signed infinite limit of matching quotient form, $g'$ is nonzero on the punctured approach region, and $f'/g'\to L\in\overline{\mathbb R}$. Apply the quotient Cauchy theorem between a fixed base point and the variable point. Divide by $g(x)$ and use $g(a)/g(x)\to0$ and $f(a)/g(x)\to0$. Spell out sign/order estimates for infinite $L$ rather than performing algebra with $\infty$.

items.title: Taylor polynomials and their remainders
items.strategy: For $f$ with derivatives through order $n$ at $a$, define $T_{n,a}f(x)=\sum_{j\le n}f^{(j)}(a)(x-a)^j/\iota(j!)$ and $R_{n,a}f(x)=f(x)-T_{n,a}f(x)$. The factorial in the plan is a natural finite product; explicitly embed it in $\mathbb R$ before division and prove it is positive. Cover $n=0$ and $x=a$.

items.title: Taylor polynomials match the prescribed derivatives at the centre
items.strategy: Differentiate each finite monomial sum and prove for $0\le r\le n$ that $(T_{n,a}f)^{(r)}(a)=f^{(r)}(a)$. Track falling factorials and cancel their embedded real values, including the cases $r=0$, $j=r$, and $j<r$. Conclude that the Taylor remainder and its first $n$ derivatives vanish at $a$.

items.title: Taylor's Schlömilch–Roche remainder formula
items.strategy: For $a\ne x$, define $\Phi(t)=f(x)-\sum_{j=0}^n f^{(j)}(t)(x-t)^j/\iota(j!)$ and $\Psi(t)=(x-t)^p$. Differentiate the finite sum: all adjacent terms telescope, leaving $\Phi'(t)=-f^{(n+1)}(t)(x-t)^n/\iota(n!)$, while $\Psi'(t)=-\iota(p)(x-t)^{p-1}$. Apply the Cauchy mean-value quotient theorem once on the interval from $a$ to $x$, use the endpoint values, and reflect the argument when $x<a$. Restrict $p$ to naturals with $1\le p\le n+1$; the formula concerns only $x\ne a$ because no point lies strictly between equal endpoints.

items.title: The Lagrange and Cauchy forms of Taylor's remainder
items.strategy: In the Schlömilch–Roche formula set $p=n+1$ to obtain $R=f^{(n+1)}(\xi)(x-a)^{n+1}/\iota((n+1)!)$, and set $p=1$ to obtain the Cauchy form $R=f^{(n+1)}(\xi)(x-\xi)^n(x-a)/\iota(n!)$. Check both substitutions using the factorial recursion and the exponent-zero convention.

items.title: Peano's form: the normalized Taylor remainder tends to zero
items.strategy: If $f$ is $n$ times differentiable on a neighbourhood of $a$, prove $R_{n,a}f(x)/(x-a)^n\to0$ as $x\to a$ for $n\ge1$. Avoid introducing unproved little-$o$ notation: state the quotient limit explicitly. Induct on $n$. Apply Cauchy's mean-value theorem to $R_{n,a}f(t)$ and $(t-a)^n$ between $a$ and $x$; the resulting quotient is the order-$(n-1)$ normalized Taylor remainder of $f'$ at an intermediate point, divided by $n$, and tends to $0$ by the induction hypothesis. This proof does not assume continuity of $f^{(n)}$. State the $n=0$ continuity analogue separately.

items.title: A uniform derivative bound gives a uniform Taylor remainder bound
items.strategy: If $|f^{(n+1)}(t)|\le M$ between $a$ and $x$, use the Lagrange remainder to prove $|R_{n,a}f(x)|\le M|x-a|^{n+1}/\iota((n+1)!)$. Include $x=a$, the sign of the embedded factorial, and the symmetric case $x<a$.

items.title: The second-derivative test for strict local extrema
items.strategy: Assume $f'(a)=0$ and $f''$ exists and is continuous near $a$. If $f''(a)>0$, continuity gives $f''>0$ nearby, so $f'$ is strictly increasing and changes sign at $a$; the first-derivative monotonicity theorem gives a strict local minimum. Treat $f''(a)<0$ symmetrically and state explicitly that $f''(a)=0$ is inconclusive.

items.title: The first nonzero higher derivative classifies a stationary point
items.strategy: Suppose derivatives through order $r$ exist near $a$, all orders $1$ through $r-1$ vanish at $a$, and $f^{(r)}(a)\ne0$. Peano's formula makes the sign of $f(x)-f(a)$ equal to the sign of $f^{(r)}(a)(x-a)^r$ sufficiently near $a$. Conclude: even $r$ gives a strict minimum or maximum according to the sign, while odd $r$ gives neither. Keep $r\ge2$ and the punctured two-sided neighbourhood explicit.

items.title: If $f'(a)=f''(a)=0$, then the second derivative test still decides whether $a$ is an extremum
items.strategy: Refute the statement by recording that the hypotheses alone allow a strict minimum, a strict maximum, or no extremum. The companion page supplies $x^4$, $-x^4$, and $x^3$. Explain that the valid theorem requires a nonzero first higher derivative; do not label the inconclusive case as a failed theorem.

items.title: Scope, endpoint, factorial, and deferred-remainder conventions
items.strategy: Record the one-sided endpoint convention, the $\mathbb N$-contains-$0$ convention, and the natural-to-real embedding on factorial/binomial coefficients. State that the integral remainder is deferred to the later integration page; Borel's theorem and Dini derivatives are not asserted because their machinery is outside the declared closure. Explicitly reject the false Darboux-plus-Baire-one continuity claim.

title: Darboux, L'Hôpital, and Taylor's Theorem: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: A bounded $C^1$ periodic oscillator made from a quartic Hermite spline
items.strategy: For $t\in\mathbb R$, let $m=\lfloor t\rfloor$, $u=t-m\in[0,1)$, and set $q(t)=u^2(1-u)^2$. Prove the value and first derivative glue at integer endpoints, so $q$ is bounded, nonconstant, $1$-periodic and $C^1$, with $q'(t)=2u(1-u)(1-2u)$ off the integers and the same formula extending there. This replaces trigonometric oscillators and uses the published integer-part theorem.

items.title: A differentiable function whose derivative is discontinuous
items.strategy: Using the periodic polynomial $q$, set $f(0)=0$ and $f(x)=x^2q(1/x)$ for $x\ne0$. Boundedness of $q$ gives $f(x)/x\to0$, so $f'(0)=0$. Away from $0$, compute $f'(x)=2xq(1/x)-q'(1/x)$. Choose two sequences of reciprocal points with different fractional parts to show $f'$ has no limit at $0$, while Darboux's theorem still forces every intermediate derivative value.

items.title: For every $k\ge0$, $x^k|x|$ is $C^k$ but not $C^{k+1}$
items.strategy: Treat the two sides as $x^{k+1}$ and $-x^{k+1}$ with the parity accounted for by $|x|$. Differentiate through order $k$: all one-sided values glue continuously and vanish at $0$. At order $k+1$ the one-sided constants differ, so that derivative does not exist at $0$. This is the corrected family; the source-plan expression $x^{k+1}|x|$ is off by one.

items.title: A function with positive derivative at $0$ that is monotone on no neighbourhood of $0$
items.strategy: Let $F(0)=0$ and $F(x)=x+A x^2q(1/x)$ for $x\ne0$, where $q$ is the periodic polynomial oscillator and choose an explicit natural $A$ large enough (for example $A=10$ after evaluating $q'$ at $u=1/5$). Boundedness gives $F'(0)=1$. Along reciprocal sequences the term $-Aq'(1/x)$ makes $F'$ negative at arbitrarily small points, ruling out nondecreasing behaviour by the MVT; $F'(0)>0$ rules out nonincreasing behaviour directly from the derivative definition.

items.title: L'Hôpital evaluates $\lim_{x\to1}(x^3-x)/(x^2-1)$ as $1$
items.strategy: Verify the $0/0$ hypotheses on a punctured neighbourhood of $1$, differentiate numerator and denominator, and simplify the derivative quotient to $(3x^2-1)/(2x)$, whose limit is $1$. Cross-check by factoring the original quotient to $x$ off $x=1$. The factorization is included to expose every cancellation rather than treating the rule as a black box.

items.title: L'Hôpital's conclusion does not imply convergence of the derivative quotient
items.strategy: Set $f(0)=g(0)=0$, $g(x)=x$, and $f(x)=x+x^2q(1/x)$ for $x\ne0$. Then $f(x)/g(x)=1+xq(1/x)\to1$, but $f'(x)/g'(x)=1+2xq(1/x)-q'(1/x)$ has two different subsequential limits. Verify $g'=1$ and every forward theorem hypothesis except derivative-ratio convergence. This is a log-free, trigonometry-free converse failure.

items.title: The Taylor polynomial of $(1-x)^{-1}$ at $0$ has the exact geometric remainder $x^{n+1}/(1-x)$
items.strategy: For $x\ne1$, use the finite geometric identity $(1-x)\sum_{j\le n}x^j=1-x^{n+1}$. Prove by induction that the $j$-th derivative at $0$ is $\iota(j!)$, so the Taylor polynomial is exactly the finite geometric sum. Deduce the exact remainder and compare it with the Lagrange bound on a fixed interval $|x|\le r<1$.

items.title: The functions $x^4$, $-x^4$, and $x^3$ show that $f''(0)=0$ is inconclusive
items.strategy: Compute the first two derivatives at $0$. Order of powers shows that $x^4$ has a strict minimum, $-x^4$ has a strict maximum, and $x^3$ has neither. Apply the first-nonzero-derivative test at orders $4,4,3$ and explicitly discharge the false statement's common hypotheses.

items.title: The real exponential function and the number $e$ by a power series
items.strategy: Define $\exp x=\sum_{n\ge0}x^n/\iota(n!)$ and $e=\exp(1)$. Keep the natural factorial of the finite-counting page distinct from its positive real embedding. The definition is provisional until convergence for every real $x$ is proved in the next item; do not use logarithms or real powers.

items.title: The exponential series converges absolutely for every real argument
items.strategy: Fix $x$. Choose a natural $N>2|x|$ by Archimedes. Beyond $N$, consecutive absolute terms shrink by at least $1/2$, so the tail is dominated by a geometric series. Conclude absolute convergence and hence convergence; equivalently the power series has infinite radius. State the factorial recurrence only after embedding it into $\mathbb R$.

items.title: The exponential addition formula $\exp(x+y)=\exp(x)\exp(y)$
items.strategy: Multiply the two absolutely convergent exponential series using the published Cauchy-product theorem. For coefficient $n$, use the binomial theorem and $\binom{n}{k}/(k!(n-k)!)=1/n!$ after embedding every natural coefficient into $\mathbb R$. This is the only proof of the addition law; do not appeal to an ODE before ODE uniqueness is established.

items.title: The exponential is positive and satisfies $\exp(-x)=1/\exp(x)$
items.strategy: The addition formula gives $\exp(x)\exp(-x)=\exp(0)=1$, so neither factor is zero. Also $\exp(x)=\exp(x/2)^2$ is nonnegative; being nonzero, it is positive. Conclude the reciprocal identity. This proof works for negative $x$ without termwise sign estimates.

items.title: The exponential function is smooth and $(\exp)'=\exp$
items.strategy: Use the infinite radius and the published termwise-differentiation theorem. Shift the derivative series and cancel the embedded factor $\iota(n+1)$ against $\iota((n+1)!)$ to recover the original series. Invoke the power-series smoothness theorem for all higher derivatives.

items.title: The exponential function is strictly increasing
items.strategy: For $x<y$, apply the mean-value theorem to obtain $\exp(y)-\exp(x)=\exp(c)(y-x)$ for some $c\in(x,y)$. Positivity makes the right side strictly positive. Record continuity from the power-series theorem and do not infer strict increase merely from a nonnegative derivative.

items.title: The exponential tends to $+\infty$ at $+\infty$ and to $0$ at $-\infty$
items.strategy: For $x\ge0$, the first two series terms give $\exp x\ge1+x$, hence divergence to $+\infty$. Use $\exp(-x)=1/\exp x$ for the negative limit. Conclude that the range is contained in the positive reals and approaches both endpoints of that interval. Use the definitions of limits at infinity rather than informal asymptotics.

items.title: The exponential is a continuous bijection from $\mathbb R$ onto $(0,\infty)$
items.strategy: Strict increase gives injectivity. Given $y>0$, the two endpoint limits give $a<b$ with $\exp(a)<y<\exp(b)$, and the intermediate-value theorem gives a preimage. Positivity excludes every nonpositive value. Do not name the inverse logarithm on this page.

items.title: The exponential dominates every fixed nonnegative integer power at $+\infty$
items.strategy: For $m\in\mathbb N$, $a>0$ and $x>0$, retain the $(m+1)$-st nonnegative term of the series for $\exp(ax)$ to get $\exp(ax)\ge (ax)^{m+1}/\iota((m+1)!)$. Hence $0\le x^m/\exp(ax)\le\iota((m+1)!)/(a^{m+1}x)\to0$. State only domination of fixed nonnegative integer powers.

items.title: The exponential is the unique solution of $y'=y$ with $y(0)=1$
items.strategy: Existence is the derivative theorem and $\exp(0)=1$. For uniqueness, if $y'=y$, differentiate $y(x)\exp(-x)$ using product and chain rules; its derivative is zero, so the product is constant and equals $1$. Positivity permits division. Include the interval-local version with an arbitrary initial value $y(a)=c$, yielding $y(x)=c\exp(x-a)$.

items.title: Regular normalized multiplicative Cauchy equations characterize the exponential
items.strategy: Prove two clauses. First, if $F(x+y)=F(x)F(y)$ and $F$ is differentiable at $0$ with $F(0)=1$ and $F'(0)=1$, then a translated difference quotient gives $F'=F$, so IVP uniqueness gives $F=\exp$. Second, if $F$ is continuous, multiplicative, and $F(1)=e$, then $F>0$, agrees with $\exp$ on rationals by uniqueness of positive roots, and agrees everywhere by density and continuity. Treat the identically-zero multiplicative solution separately before asserting $F(0)=1$.

items.title: For fixed $k$, $\binom{n}{k}/n^k$ tends to $1/k!$
items.strategy: For $n\ge k$, use the proved closed formula to write $\iota\binom{n}{k}/\iota(n)^k=(1/\iota(k!))\prod_{j<k}(1-\iota(j)/\iota(n))$. Each factor lies in $[0,1]$ and tends to $1$, so the product tends to $1$ and the coefficient is uniformly between $0$ and $1/\iota(k!)$. Include $k=0$ and state the natural-to-real embeddings at every division.

items.title: For every real $x$, $(1+x/n)^n\to\exp x$
items.strategy: Take $n>|x|$ so the base is positive and expand by the binomial theorem. For a fixed finite head, the scaled-binomial lemma gives convergence to the corresponding exponential terms. Bound the remaining binomial tail uniformly by the tail of $\sum |x|^k/k!$, then choose the head by convergence of that series. This finite-head/infinite-tail proof works for negative $x$ and contains no logarithm.

items.title: Picard iteration from $1$ produces the exponential partial sums
items.strategy: Define $P_0(x)=1$ and $P_{n+1}(x)=1+\int_0^xP_n(t)\,dt$. Inductively use the power rule and the working FTC to prove $P_n(x)=\sum_{k\le n}x^k/\iota(k!)$. Uniform convergence on compact intervals gives $P_n\to\exp$, and the uniform-limit integration theorem yields $\exp(x)=1+\int_0^x\exp(t)dt$. Conversely differentiate that integral equation to recover the IVP.

items.title: The power-series, product-limit, IVP, functional-equation, and Picard definitions agree
items.strategy: Collect the preceding results as an equivalence theorem: E1 is the defining series; E2 is the product limit; E3 is the normalized IVP; E6 is either regular normalized multiplicative Cauchy condition; and E11 is the Picard integral iteration. For each arrow cite the theorem that already proves it rather than repeating proofs. State the normalization in every formulation so no one-parameter family is accidentally identified with $\exp$.

items.title: A geometric bound for tails of the exponential series
items.strategy: For real $x$ and $N$ with $\iota(N+2)\ge2|x|$, consecutive absolute terms after index $N+1$ have ratio at most $1/2$. Compare the tail with the geometric series of ratio $1/2$ to obtain $\sum_{k=N+1}^{\infty}|x|^k/\iota(k!)\le2|x|^{N+1}/\iota((N+1)!)$.

items.title: The elementary numerical bound $2<e<3$
items.strategy: The first two terms and the positive remaining tail give $e>2$. For the upper bound apply the factorial-tail estimate at $n=1$ carefully (or sum the sharper geometric comparison beginning with $1/2!$) to obtain a strict bound below $3$. Avoid decimal approximations.

items.title: The number $e$ is irrational
items.strategy: Assume $e=p/q$ with integers $p$ and positive $q$. Choose a natural $n>q$. Then $\iota(n!)e$ and $\iota(n!)\sum_{k\le n}1/k!$ are integers, so their positive difference is an integer. The factorial-tail bound makes it strictly between $0$ and $1$, a contradiction. Prove the divisibility/cancellation step with the factorial definition and identify integer and real embeddings explicitly.

items.title: The exponential roadmap and its circularity hazards
items.strategy: Record the five equivalent constructions proved here and the proof order: series before addition, addition before positivity, derivative before IVP uniqueness, and all of these before characterization. State that logarithms and arbitrary real powers are deferred. Distinguish the published rational-power operation from $\exp(x\log a)$, which is unavailable. Record that the compact bump is in the companion page but a general smooth partition of unity and a nowhere-analytic smooth function are outside this dependency-closed scope.

title: The Exponential Function: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: The log-free product limit $(1-2/n)^n\to\exp(-2)$
items.strategy: Apply the product-limit theorem at $x=-2$, noting that the base is positive for $n>2$. Expand several finite cases only as a sanity check; the proof uses the general finite-head/tail theorem, not a nonexistent logarithm of a negative or zero base.

items.title: The convergence $(1+x/n)^n\to\exp x$ is not uniform on $\mathbb R$
items.strategy: For each $n$, evaluate at $x=n$. The approximant is $2^n$, whereas $\exp(n)=e^n$ by repeated use of the addition formula. Since $e>2$, the difference is at least $e^n-2^n$ and does not tend to zero. State uniform convergence using the published definition and note that the base is positive at these witnesses.

items.title: The one-sided flat function is $C^\infty$ with identically zero Taylor series
items.strategy: Define $\phi(x)=\exp(-1/x^2)$ for $x>0$ and $\phi(x)=0$ for $x\le0$. Inductively show on $x>0$ that $\phi^{(n)}(x)=P_n(1/x)\exp(-1/x^2)$ for a polynomial $P_n$. Exponential domination makes every one-sided derivative limit at $0$ equal $0$, so all derivatives glue and vanish there. The function is positive for $x>0$, hence differs from its zero Maclaurin series in every right neighbourhood.

items.title: A nonzero smooth compactly supported bump
items.strategy: Define $\psi(x)=\exp(-1/(1-x^2))$ for $|x|<1$ and $0$ for $|x|\ge1$. On the open interval smoothness follows from the chain and algebra rules. At $\pm1$, reduce each one-sided derivative to the flat-function estimate after factoring $1-x^2$ and prove all derivatives tend to $0$. Conclude $\psi\in C^\infty$, is positive on $(-1,1)$, and has support $[-1,1]$. Do not claim a general partition of unity.

items.title: A discontinuous positive solution of $F(x+y)=F(x)F(y)$
items.strategy: Assuming the Axiom of Choice, extend the $\mathbb Q$-independent set $\{1,\alpha\}$ to a Hamel basis of $\mathbb R$ over $\mathbb Q$. Define an additive non-linear $h$ by assigning incompatible basis values, and put $F=\exp\circ h$. The addition formula makes $F$ positive and multiplicative. If $F$ were continuous, strict injectivity of $\exp$ would force enough regularity on $h$ to contradict its construction; alternatively use the normalized functional-equation theorem after rescaling. State the choice cost explicitly.

items.title: The exponential is not uniformly continuous on $\mathbb R$
items.strategy: Take $x_n=n$ and $y_n=n+1/n$. Their distance tends to $0$, but the MVT gives $\exp(y_n)-\exp(x_n)=\exp(c_n)/n\ge e^n/n$, which is bounded away from $0$ and in fact diverges. Justify the last growth from exponential domination. Contrast with Heine–Cantor on every compact interval.

title: The Riemann Integral in R^m and Jordan Content

items.title: Axis-parallel rectangles in $\mathbb R^m$ and their volume
items.strategy: Fix $m\geq1$. For vectors $a,b\in\mathbb R^m$ with $a_j\leq b_j$, define $[a,b]=\{x:a_j\leq x_j\leq b_j\text{ for }j<m\}$ and $\operatorname{vol}([a,b])=\prod_{j<m}(b_j-a_j)$. Call the rectangle nondegenerate when every inequality is strict. The finite product is the published recursive product, so volume exists; prove nonnegativity and the effect of a coordinate cut. State that at $m=1$ this is the published interval and its length.

items.title: Grid partitions of a rectangle in $\mathbb R^m$, their cells, refinements and mesh
items.strategy: A grid partition is a list of one-dimensional partitions indexed by $j<m$. Its cells are indexed by the multi-indices $i\in\mathbb N^m$ satisfying $i_j<n_j$, and each cell is the product of the corresponding subintervals. Define every sum over cells as an iterated finite sum, recursively in the $m$ coordinate index ranges; this avoids importing the finite-index-set sum from a page outside the fixed prerequisite closure. Define the mesh as the maximum coordinate subinterval length; by the norm/metric dictionary this is the $d_\infty$ diameter of the largest cell. Define coordinatewise refinement and common refinement, prove the cells cover the rectangle with disjoint interiors, and prove by induction on $m$ that the iterated sum of cell volumes is the rectangle volume. No multidimensional partition or sum may be left as an informal picture.

items.title: Lower and upper Darboux sums over a grid partition in $\mathbb R^m$
items.strategy: For bounded $f$ on a nondegenerate rectangle and each grid cell $Q_i$, take $m_i=\inf f[Q_i]$ and $M_i=\sup f[Q_i]$, then form the iterated finite sums of $m_i\operatorname{vol}(Q_i)$ and $M_i\operatorname{vol}(Q_i)$ fixed in the grid definition. Prove the extrema exist, the sums are finite reals, and lower sum $\leq$ upper sum. Record that the gap is the corresponding iterated sum of cell oscillations times cell volumes.

items.title: Refinement raises multidimensional lower sums and lowers upper sums, with a quantitative boundary-slab estimate
items.strategy: For one inserted coordinate hyperplane, split the relevant coordinate sum and group the resulting iterated finite sums inside each old cell to prove monotonicity. Iterate coordinatewise for a general refinement. Add the quantitative clause needed for mesh-based Riemann sums: after refining an arbitrary fine grid by one fixed grid, only cells meeting the fixed interior hyperplanes can change the coarse Darboux bounds; their total volume is bounded by a fixed cross-sectional constant times the fine mesh. Prove that slab bound by induction and finite-product distributivity rather than appealing to measure or to sums over abstract finite sets.

items.title: The lower and upper Darboux integrals over a nondegenerate rectangle in $\mathbb R^m$
items.strategy: On a nondegenerate rectangle, take the supremum of all lower grid sums and infimum of all upper grid sums, and call $f$ integrable when they agree. The endpoint grids are nonempty, refinement bounds the two sum families, and completeness plus the infimum theorem supplies the extrema. Do not define an integral on degenerate rectangles, because the grid definition requires strict coordinate partitions.

items.title: Riemann's criterion on a nondegenerate rectangle in $\mathbb R^m$: integrability is equivalent to arbitrarily small Darboux gaps
items.strategy: On a nondegenerate rectangle, repeat the published supremum/infimum argument with grid partitions: equality of the lower and upper integrals gives grids good for the two sides and their common refinement is good for both. Conversely one small Darboux gap bounds the integral gap.

items.title: Tagged grid partitions and Riemann sums in $\mathbb R^m$
items.strategy: A tagging assigns one point to each multi-indexed grid cell. A canonical lower-corner tagging proves existence without choice; when arbitrary cellwise selections are needed, enumerate the finitely nested coordinate ranges and apply finite choice inductively. Define $S(f,P,\xi)$ by the iterated finite-sum convention of the grid definition. Define mesh convergence to $I$ by requiring every tagged grid of sufficiently small mesh to have sum near $I$. Prove each Riemann sum lies between the Darboux sums of the same grid.

items.title: The multidimensional Darboux and tagged-mesh definitions of the Riemann integral agree
items.strategy: The easy direction traps every tagged sum between the Darboux sums of one grid. For the converse, choose a fixed grid with small Darboux gap, refine an arbitrary sufficiently fine grid by it, and use the quantitative boundary-slab estimate to control the change in upper and lower sums. Choose near-extremal tags cellwise by finite choice, exactly as the published one-dimensional proof does. This is a long proof already decomposed by the refinement lemma; do not rebuild that estimate inside the theorem.

items.title: At $m=1$, nondegenerate multidimensional rectangles, grid sums and the integral are exactly the published one-dimensional notions
items.strategy: Identify $\mathbb R^1$ with $\mathbb R$. Nondegeneracy is exactly $a<b$; a coordinate grid is one ordinary partition, its cells are the published subintervals, volume is length, and both Darboux and tagged sums agree term for term. Conclude that the integrability classes and values coincide.

items.title: Linearity, monotonicity, the absolute-value estimate and coordinate-slice additivity for the Riemann integral in $\mathbb R^m$
items.strategy: On a nondegenerate rectangle prove linearity and monotonicity from Darboux gaps and identify values through tagged-sum convergence; derive $|\int f|\le\int|f|$. For a strictly interior coordinate cut, splice coordinate partitions and split the nested finite sum to obtain additivity and the converse integrability statement. Endpoint cuts are excluded because they create degenerate subrectangles, for which this integral is not defined.

items.title: Every continuous function on a closed nondegenerate rectangle in $\mathbb R^m$ is Riemann integrable
items.strategy: A closed nondegenerate rectangle is compact by Heine-Borel. Metric Heine-Cantor makes a continuous scalar function uniformly continuous, and the extreme-value theorem makes it bounded. A grid below the uniform-continuity threshold has small oscillation on every cell, so the multidimensional Riemann criterion applies.

items.title: Measure zero and content zero in $\mathbb R^m$ by countable and finite cube covers
items.strategy: For $m\geq1$, define a closed axis-parallel cube and its volume. A set is null when for every $\varepsilon>0$ it has a countable cube cover whose volume series is at most $\varepsilon$; it has content zero when a finite such cover exists. Cube covers are chosen because Lipschitz images are controlled by cubes without aspect-ratio defects. Prove inheritance by subsets and finite-cover padding. Do not define Lebesgue measure or outer measure.

items.title: At $m=1$, cube-nullity and cube-content-zero are exactly the published interval-cover notions
items.strategy: Under the isometry $\mathbb R^1\cong\mathbb R$, a closed cube is a closed interval and its volume is its length. The countable and finite cover quantifiers, including their finite-sum and series bounds, are therefore word for word those of the published definition. Record both directions explicitly so later items may move between the vocabularies.

items.title: Subsets and countable unions of null subsets of $\mathbb R^m$ are null
items.strategy: Subset closure is immediate. For a sequence of null sets, assign the $j$-th set a geometric fraction of the $\varepsilon$ budget, use countable choice to select one cube cover for each set, and enumerate the doubly indexed cubes through the published bijection $\mathbb N^2\to\mathbb N$. Bound finite partial sums by finite rectangles of indices, as the published one-dimensional theorem does. State the countable-choice cost in the theorem.

items.title: For compact subsets of $\mathbb R^m$, measure zero and content zero coincide
items.strategy: Content zero implies nullity by padding. Conversely enlarge every closed covering cube slightly to an open cube, spending a geometric fraction of the remaining volume budget; compactness gives a finite subcover, and bounding its finitely many indices controls the total enlarged volume. Use Heine–Borel only to identify compact sets when needed, not as a substitute for the finite-subcover definition.

items.title: Oscillation of a real function on subsets of $\mathbb R^m$ and at a point
items.strategy: For $f:A\to\mathbb R$ define $\omega_f(S)=\sup\{|f(x)-f(y)|:x,y\in S\}$ in the extended reals and $\omega_f(c)=\inf_{r>0}\omega_f(A\cap B(c,r))$, using Euclidean balls. Prove well-posedness and monotonicity under inclusion as in the published real-domain definition. Include the dictionary clause that under $\mathbb R^1\cong\mathbb R$ this is exactly `def-oscillation`.

items.title: A function on a subset of $\mathbb R^m$ is continuous at $x$ iff its oscillation there is $0$, and every oscillation superlevel set is closed
items.strategy: Translate the epsilon definition of metric continuity into small oscillation on a ball for one direction; for the other, use one point fixed at $x$ in the oscillation bound. To prove $\{x:\omega_f(x)\geq\varepsilon\}$ closed relative to the domain, show its complement is open: one ball with oscillation below $\varepsilon$ works for every sufficiently nearby centre after shrinking the radius. State the result for bounded $f$ when real-valued oscillations are needed by integration.

items.title: A finite rectangle cover admits grid control with arbitrarily small volume excess
items.strategy: Enlarge each cube in a given finite cover by a positive margin so that the sum of the enlarged volumes increases by less than a prescribed $\eta$; continuity of the finitely many integer-power volume functions at margin $0$ supplies the choice. Take the minimum of the finitely many positive margins, insert every enlarged-cube endpoint into the corresponding coordinate partition, and pass to a common refinement of mesh below that minimum. Every refined cell meeting the originally covered set then lies inside one of the enlarged cubes. Split the iterated cell sum along the aligned endpoints to bound the total volume of those cells by the sum of the enlarged-cube volumes. Treat closed-cell boundary overlap explicitly. This is the cover-to-grid lemma used twice in the multidimensional Lebesgue criterion.

items.title: Lebesgue's criterion in $\mathbb R^m$: a bounded function on a closed nondegenerate rectangle is Riemann integrable iff its discontinuity set is null
items.strategy: On a closed nondegenerate rectangle, prove sufficiency using compact oscillation superlevels, finite cube covers, grid control, and one uniform mesh on the compact complement. For necessity, a small Darboux gap bounds the total volume of high-oscillation cells. Prove directly that every finite family of axis-parallel rectangles, degenerate ones included, has finite cube covers with total volume arbitrarily close to its rectangle-volume sum, using one common cube side, the integer-part theorem, and polynomial continuity. This converts both the high cells and grid-hyperplane pieces to content-zero covers; countable-union closure then handles the full discontinuity set.

items.title: Jordan inner and outer content and Jordan measurable bounded sets in $\mathbb R^m$
items.strategy: For metric-bounded $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, derive a nondegenerate coordinate bounding box from a Euclidean ball. Define outer content by finite rectangle covers and inner content by finite interior-disjoint inscribed families. The box makes the extrema finite; refining endpoints proves every inner sum is at most every outer sum. Define Jordan measurability by equality and handle empty and degenerate sets explicitly.

items.title: A bounded set is Jordan measurable iff its indicator is Riemann integrable, and the integral is its Jordan content
items.strategy: Choose a nondegenerate bounding rectangle. Indicator lower and upper grid sums are the inner and outer grid approximations. Compare arbitrary finite rectangle approximations with grid approximations by small enlargement or shrinking. Coordinate additivity in a larger rectangle proves that integrability and value are independent of the chosen nondegenerate bound.

items.title: A bounded set in $\mathbb R^m$ is Jordan measurable iff its boundary is null, equivalently of content zero
items.strategy: The indicator of $E$ is discontinuous exactly at $\partial E$. Apply the multidimensional Lebesgue criterion on a nondegenerate bounding rectangle. Metric boundedness supplies a closed bounding box containing $\overline E$; the boundary is closed and therefore compact by Heine-Borel. Compact nullity is equivalent to content zero.

items.title: The Riemann integral of a bounded function over a bounded Jordan measurable set
items.strategy: Let $E$ be metric-bounded and Jordan measurable and $f:E\to\mathbb R$ bounded. Choose a nondegenerate bounding rectangle, extend $f$ by $0$, and define integrability and the integral through that extension. Record bounding-rectangle independence in `justified_by`; for $f=1$ recover Jordan content.

items.title: The Riemann integral over a Jordan set is independent of the bounding rectangle
items.strategy: Place two nondegenerate bounding rectangles strictly inside a larger nondegenerate rectangle. Strict coordinate cuts decompose the larger rectangle into the chosen box and nondegenerate added pieces. Coordinate-slice additivity shows that extending by zero preserves integrability and value, and comparison through the common larger box proves independence.

items.title: A continuous real function on a compact Jordan measurable set is Riemann integrable over that set
items.strategy: Treat the empty set separately; otherwise the metric extreme-value theorem makes $f$ bounded. In a nondegenerate bounding rectangle the zero extension can be discontinuous only on $\partial E$, which is null by the Jordan criterion. The multidimensional Lebesgue criterion makes the extension integrable.

items.title: Jordan content is finitely additive when the overlap has content zero
items.strategy: For Jordan measurable bounded $E,F$ with $E\cap F$ of content zero, use $1_{E\cup F}=1_E+1_F-1_{E\cap F}$ and multidimensional linearity. The indicator of a content-zero set has integral $0$ by the indicator theorem. State the disjoint case explicitly and obtain finite families by induction, not by a count in prose.

items.title: A Lipschitz map $\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^m$ sends null sets to null sets
items.strategy: Cover the null set by cubes. A cube of side $\ell$ has Euclidean diameter at most $\iota(m)\ell$ using the norm comparisons. An $L$-Lipschitz image of it lies in a cube of side $2L\iota(m)\ell$, whose volume is the fixed factor $(2L\iota(m))^m$ times the original volume. Allocate the input cover the corresponding scaled $\varepsilon$ budget and sum. Treat $L=0$ separately. Restrict to equal domain and codomain dimensions; the statement is false across arbitrary dimensions.

items.title: The graph of a continuous function on a closed nondegenerate rectangle in $\mathbb R^m$ has content zero in $\mathbb R^{m+1}$
items.strategy: Uniform continuity gives a sufficiently fine coordinate grid on the domain for which the vertical oscillation of $f$ on each cell is small. Above each domain cell, stack finitely many $(m+1)$-dimensional cubes whose side is the grid scale; the integer-part lemma bounds the number of cubes by the vertical oscillation divided by that scale plus a fixed endpoint allowance. Summed over the domain grid, their total volume is bounded by a fixed rectangle-dependent constant times the oscillation bound plus the grid scale, and therefore can be made arbitrarily small. This produces the cube covers required by `def-null-and-content-zero-in-rn`, not merely skinny rectangle covers. State $m\geq1$; no metric on $\mathbb R^0$ is needed.

items.title: If every finite interval cover of $A\subseteq\mathbb R$ has total length at least $c$, then every rectangle cover of $A\times[0,d]$ has total area at least $cd$
items.strategy: List a finite rectangle cover and clip it to a bounding rectangle, then partition $[0,d]$ at all listed vertical endpoints. On each resulting horizontal strip, choose an interior height; the horizontal projections of the covering rectangles active there cover $A$, so their widths total at least $c$. Multiply by the strip height and sum. Reindex the resulting nested finite sums using splitting and distributivity. This elementary product estimate supplies the positive-content claim in the compact and open counterexamples without using Fubini or abstract finite-index-set sums.

items.title: Conventions and proved scope for the Riemann integral in $\mathbb R^m$ and Jordan content
items.strategy: Record $m\geq1$, axis-parallel grids, cube covers for nullity, arbitrary finite rectangle covers for Jordan outer content, and both one-dimensional agreement results. State that `thm-lebesgue-criterion-in-rn` uses only cover-nullity and no Lebesgue measure. Record the proved Lipschitz-image theorem. Say only that a continuously differentiable image theorem is not asserted on this page; do not mention an unbuilt total derivative as though it were a dependency.

title: The Riemann Integral in R^m and Jordan Content: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: The unit box in $\mathbb R^m$ has volume $1$, and the integral of a constant $c$ over it is $c$
items.strategy: Every side length is $1$, so the finite product volume is $1$, including the indexing check over $j<m$. On every grid, the lower and upper sums of the constant function coincide with $c$ times the sum of cell volumes, hence with $c$. This is a direct computation from the definitions, not an appeal to iterated integration.

items.title: The rational points of $[0,1]^2$ form a bounded null set that is not Jordan measurable
items.strategy: The set $(\mathbb Q\cap[0,1])^2$ is countable, using countability of $\mathbb Q$ and the published pairing of naturals, hence null by the countable-union lemma applied to singleton cubes. Density of the rationals and irrationals in each coordinate makes both the set and its complement dense in the square, so its boundary is the whole square. The unit square is not null, and the Jordan boundary criterion gives non-measurability. This is the bounded plane set without area.

items.title: The Smith–Volterra–Cantor slab $S\times[0,1]$ is compact and not Jordan measurable
items.strategy: The fat Cantor set $S$ is compact, nowhere dense, and every interval cover has total length at least $1/2$. The product slab is closed and bounded in $\mathbb R^2$, hence compact, and has empty interior, so it equals its boundary. The product lower-bound lemma gives Jordan outer content at least $1/2$ for that boundary. The boundary criterion therefore rules out Jordan measurability. No product measure or Fubini theorem is used.

items.title: $((0,1)\setminus S)\times(0,1)$ is bounded and open, but its boundary has positive Jordan outer content
items.strategy: The complement of the closed fat Cantor set inside $(0,1)$ is open, so the product is open and bounded. Its boundary contains $S\times[0,1]$ (verify neighbourhood intersections with the open set using nowhere density and with its complement using membership in $S$). Outer-content monotonicity and the slab lower bound give a positive lower bound for the boundary, so the open set is not Jordan measurable.

items.title: The parabola segment $\{(x,x^2):0\leq x\leq1\}$ has content zero in $\mathbb R^2$
items.strategy: Apply the graph theorem to the continuous polynomial $x\mapsto x^2$ on $[0,1]$. Also give the direct uniform-grid estimate: on an interval of width $1/\iota(N)$ the vertical oscillation is at most $2/\iota(N)$, so rectangles covering the graph have total area tending to $0$. Write every reciprocal of a natural through $\iota$.

items.title: The right triangle $\{(x,y)\in[0,1]^2:x+y\leq1\}$ has Jordan content $1/2$
items.strategy: Use uniform $N$-by-$N$ grids. Count cells wholly inside and cells meeting the triangle; the two staircase areas differ by at most $1/\iota(N)$ and bracket $1/2$. Prove the finite identity $\sum_{k<N}\iota(k)=\iota(N)\iota(N-1)/2$ by induction or cite a published equivalent only after reading it. The Riemann criterion for the indicator gives Jordan measurability and the common limit $1/2$. The sloping boundary also follows as a graph-content-zero check.

items.title: The Cantor slab $C\times[0,1]$ has content zero in $\mathbb R^2$
items.strategy: Cover the Cantor set by finitely many small intervals. Above an interval of width $\ell>0$, stack finitely many squares of side $\ell$; the integer-part theorem bounds their total area by $\ell+2\ell^2$. Summing gives arbitrarily small finite rectangle covers, so Jordan outer content is zero and the nonnegative inner content is squeezed to zero. Contrast with the fat-Cantor slab.

items.title: The term “rectifiable” for Jordan measurable sets is unrelated to rectifiable curves
items.strategy: Record with a checked Munkres reference that some multivariable-analysis texts call bounded sets with null boundary rectifiable. State the proposition itself: in this page's terminology these are the Jordan measurable bounded sets by the boundary criterion. Warn that this usage does not mean finite curve length and creates no dependency on the arc-length page. Keep the remark terminological and source-backed.
